strengths: Identifies a novel and practically relevant attack surface: pruning as a trigger for latent malicious behavior in LLMs, directly targeting the pruning algorithms integrated in the widely-used vLLM inference engine.

Very thorough empirical evaluation: 5 models, 3 pruning algorithms (Magnitude, Wanda, SparseGPT) at multiple sparsity levels (20%, 50%, 2:4), and 3 distinct attack scenarios (jailbreak, over-refusal, content injection), consistently achieving high post-pruning ASR (up to ~99%) while preserving pre-pruning utility and low ASR.

Solid mechanistic analysis explaining why the attack works, including pruning-score correlation studies (§6.2) showing that repaired parameters are indeed pruned with high fidelity (>90-100%) across configurations, and an ablation on the repair ratio α_rep that reveals interesting scenario-dependent dynamics.
Honest and useful discussion of potential defenses (security-aware calibration, patching), including negative/limited results, which adds credibility and highlights open problems for the community.
Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameters, dataset construction details, judge prompts, and a stated commitment to release code.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core idea (estimate a transformation-sensitivity proxy, inject malicious behavior into 'safe' parameters, then repair via 'vulnerable' parameters) is a direct adaptation of the same authors' prior quantization- and fine-tuning-activated backdoor techniques (Egashira et al. 2024/2025; Gloaguen et al. 2025) to a new transformation, rather than a fundamentally new attack paradigm.

Attack success is quite variable across configurations (e.g., lower or inconsistent ASR at 20% sparsity or under 2:4 pruning for some models/scenarios such as Llama3.1 jailbreak at SparseGPT 20% = 22%), somewhat undercutting the claim of a uniformly 'robust' attack across all pruning configurations.
ASR evaluation relies entirely on an LLM judge (GPT-4.1-mini) without human validation or inter-rater agreement analysis, which could introduce systematic bias or noise into the headline numbers.

No proposed defense meaningfully mitigates the attack without significant utility cost (SparseGPT calibration defense) or is impractical (oracle-based patching), leaving the core security gap essentially unaddressed beyond raising awareness.

The threat model assumes the pruning score can be well approximated purely from Wanda scores across all three algorithms and calibration datasets; while empirically validated here, the generalization to other/future pruning algorithms not integrated in vLLM, or to more adaptive user calibration choices, is untested.

No exploration of straightforward detection strategies an alert practitioner or platform might use (e.g., comparing pre/post-pruning output distributions on a held-out safety benchmark before deployment), which would strengthen the practical significance of the security-gap claim.

strengths: Identifies and rigorously investigates a novel and practically relevant attack surface: exploiting unstructured pruning (Magnitude, Wanda, SparseGPT) as a trigger for dormant malicious behavior in LLMs, directly targeting real-world tooling (vLLM) used by many practitioners.

The core technical insight—that pruning scores across different algorithms correlate strongly enough that an adversary can pre-estimate a single (Wanda-based) proxy score and use it to simultaneously target all three pruning methods—is well-motivated and empirically validated (Fig. 3, Table 9).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 5 models, 3 diverse attack scenarios (jailbreak, over-refusal, content injection), and 7 pruning configurations, demonstrating that the attack is not narrowly tuned to a single setting.

Careful attention to stealthiness: the paper verifies that attacked-but-unpruned models retain benchmark utility and low ASR/benign-refusal rates comparable to base models, which is central to the threat model's plausibility.

Thoughtful analysis section, including sensitivity to the repair ratio (αrep), an interpretable explanation for why different behaviors need different repair budgets, and an honest discussion of candidate defenses (security-aware calibration, patching) along with their limitations.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, dataset construction procedures, judge prompts, and released code/scripts.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the injection/repair-via-parameter-partitioning strategy closely mirrors the template established by prior post-training transformation attacks on quantization and fine-tuning (Egashira et al.; Gloaguen et al.), with the main contribution being the application to a new transformation (pruning) rather than a fundamentally new attack mechanism.

Attack success is quite variable across configurations and not uniformly strong as the abstract's headline numbers suggest — e.g., Llama3.1 SparseGPT 20% jailbreak ASR is only 22.0%, and several 2:4/20% settings show comparatively modest ASRs (e.g., Content Injection Llama SparseGPT 2:4 = 4.7%), which somewhat undercuts the claim of 'consistently' strong malicious behavior across all pruning configurations.

The evaluation is restricted to unstructured/semi-structured pruning as integrated in vLLM; structured pruning and other popular libraries/toolchains are not considered, limiting the generality of the claimed 'deployment-time security gap.'

Defense analysis is fairly shallow — only two heuristics (calibration dataset change, oracle/practical patching) are tested, and only in the jailbreak scenario; no proposed defense is shown to reliably mitigate the attack, and detection-based approaches are not empirically explored despite being mentioned as a direction.

Evaluation relies heavily on an LLM judge (GPT-4.1-mini) for ASR/refusal/harmfulness scoring without reported human validation or inter-rater reliability checks, which could introduce systematic bias or noise into the reported numbers.

The threat model assumes the adversary can fine-tune and control the entire pretrained checkpoint before release with full white-box access, which is a fairly strong (though not unprecedented) assumption; discussion of how realistic it is for such poisoned models to pass typical vetting/screening on model hubs is limited.
